In Year 7 you used the particle model to explain solids, liquids and gases, and it turns out the same model explains how heat gets from one place to another.

## Engage: the spoon

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Students who picture particles travelling up the spoon will choose that option; the bar shows energy moving while the particles stay put."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "A metal spoon stands in hot soup. Soon the handle is hot. What do you predict is happening in the spoon?"
  options: ["Hot particles travel up the handle", "Particles vibrate harder and pass the energy to their neighbours, staying in place", "Heat flows up like a liquid", "Cold leaves the spoon"]
  actual: "The particles stay in place. Those at the hot end vibrate harder and bump their neighbours, passing the energy along the handle. That is conduction."
```

## Explore: a heated bar, then heated water

```step
stage: run
insight: "The same particle colours in a solid and a liquid make the contrast clear: in the bar energy moves and particles don't; in the water both do."
try: { playground: science, starter: "boards.yml#bar", height: 520 }
tasks:
  - starter: "boards.yml#bar"
    check: { type: board, text: "Heat the bar until the far end warms up.", expect: { done: true } }
  - starter: "boards.yml#beaker"
    check: { type: board, text: "Follow a particle round one loop in the heated water.", expect: { done: true } }
```

### Conduction

Blue is cool, red is hot. Watch one particle: does it go anywhere?

### Convection

Follow the ringed particle (or click another).

## Explain: two ways to travel

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Naming the mechanism in each case (collisions passing energy; the fluid itself moving) is what makes the terms explanations, not labels."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "In the bar, how did the energy reach the far end?"
      options: ["Particles vibrated harder and bumped their neighbours, passing the energy along", "Hot particles moved to the far end", "The heater's flame travelled along the bar"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Watch a single particle: it stays in its place, just vibrating.", "Nothing but energy moved along."]
      explain: "Conduction: energy passes from particle to particle through collisions. The particles stay where they are."
    hint: ["Think about one particle in the middle of the bar: where did it go while the far end warmed up?", "Go back to the bar in Explore and keep your eye on a single dot for ten seconds, then look at the temperatures in the boxes under it."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "In the water, how did the energy reach the top?"
      options: ["The heated water itself moved up, carrying the energy", "Particles passed energy up without moving", "The cold water went down and pushed heat up"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "That happens a little (conduction), but your particle travelled the whole way round.", "Cool water does sink, but the energy is carried up by the warm water rising."]
      explain: "Convection: the heated fluid rises, carrying its energy, and cooler fluid sinks to replace it."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Why does the heated water rise?"
      options: ["Its particles spread out, so it is less dense than the cooler water around it", "Heat always rises", "Hot particles are lighter than cold ones", "The heater pushes it up"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Heat on its own does not go anywhere; something carries it. What moved up on the board?", "Each particle has the same mass hot or cold. What changes is how far apart they are.", "That is what the model does, to keep it simple. In real water nothing pushes: the warm water floats up, like a cork."]
      explain: "Heated water expands: the same particles take up more space, so it is less dense (density, from Year 7) and floats up through the cooler, denser water. The board pushes hot particles up directly; that part is a simplification."
    hint: ["On the board, what actually moved up: heat on its own, or the warm water?", "Think about what happens to the gaps between the water particles as they warm up, and what that does to how much matter is packed into each cm³."]
  - check:
      type: sort
      q: "Conduction or convection?"
      options: ["Conduction", "Convection"]
      items:
        - ["A saucepan handle getting hot", "Conduction"]
        - ["Warm air from a heater spreading round a room", "Convection"]
        - ["Your hand warming up on a hot mug", "Conduction"]
        - ["Water in a kettle heating all the way through", "Convection"]
        - ["A sea breeze on a hot afternoon", "Convection", "Air over the warm land rises; cooler air from over the sea moves in."]
        - ["Ice cream melting on a metal spoon faster than on a plastic one", "Conduction"]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Why can't convection happen in a solid?"
      options: ["The particles are held in place, so the material can't flow", "Solids can't be heated", "Particles in a solid don't move at all, so they can't carry energy"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "The bar heated up, by conduction.", "They do vibrate: that's how conduction passes energy on. They just can't change places."]
      explain: "Convection needs the material to flow. Only liquids and gases can."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Why does a foam (polystyrene) cup keep a drink hot so well?"
      options: ["It is mostly trapped air: gas particles are far apart, so there are far fewer of them to pass energy along, and air in the tiny bubbles can't flow to convect", "Its particles are packed very tightly, so energy can't squeeze through", "The foam reflects the heat back into the drink"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "It's the other way round: tightly packed particles pass energy on well by collisions. Foam is mostly widely spaced gas particles.", "Reflecting is what shiny surfaces do to radiation. Foam works by trapping air."]
      explain: "Insulators pass energy on poorly. In a gas the particles are far apart, so there are far fewer of them to pass energy along (they still collide billions of times a second), and trapping the gas in small bubbles stops convection too."
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "I explained the difference between conduction and convection, describing what the particles do in each." }
```

## Elaborate: turn the heat off

```step
stage: modify
tier: typical
insight: "Removing the heat source shows the current depends on a temperature difference: it slows and stops as the water evens out."
try: { playground: science, starter: "boards.yml#noheat", height: 560 }
check:
  type: question
  q: "Turn the heat off once the current is going and watch for a while. What happens to the current?"
  options: ["It slows down and stops as the water ends up the same temperature all through", "It keeps going forever", "It reverses direction"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "Watch the colours: once they even out, nothing is hotter or less dense than its surroundings.", "Nothing pushes it the other way: with no heat, the top still cools, and differences fade."]
  explain: "A convection current needs one part of the fluid to be hotter (less dense) than another. With no heater, the difference fades and the current stops."
```

## Elaborate: conductors and insulators

```step
stage: modify
tier: wider
insight: "Explaining insulators with both mechanisms (poor conduction, trapped air that can't convect) applies the model to real materials."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Saucepans are metal with plastic or wooden handles. Why?"
      options: ["Metal conducts heat well to cook the food; plastic and wood conduct poorly, so the handle stays cool", "Plastic handles are lighter", "Metal handles would melt"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Weight is not why: a metal handle would burn your hand.", "Metal melts at a far higher temperature than a stove reaches."]
      explain: "Metals are good conductors; plastic and wood are insulators."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Wool, fur and feathers keep animals warm mostly because they trap air. Why does trapped air insulate so well?"
      options: ["Air conducts poorly, and trapped in small pockets it can't form convection currents", "Air is warm", "Air reflects heat back"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Air is not warm in itself: it is good at not passing energy on.", "Reflecting is radiation, which shiny surfaces do. Fibres work by trapping air."]
      explain: "Gas particles are far apart, so conduction is poor; in tiny pockets the air can't circulate, so convection is blocked too. Possum-skin cloaks, made and worn by many First Nations peoples of south-eastern Australia, use the same idea: dense fur trapping air."
```

## Elaborate: a question to test

```step
stage: modify
tier: typical
insight: "Turning the trapped-air idea into an investigable question and a reasoned hypothesis uses the model to plan a test, not just explain one."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "You want to find out how wrapping a cup changes how fast hot water in it cools. Which is an investigable question?"
      options: ["Does a thicker wool wrap make hot water in a cup cool more slowly?", "Why is wool the best insulator?", "Is a wool wrap nicer to hold than a foam cup?", "What is heat?"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "That assumes the answer, and 'best' compared with what?", "'Nicer' can't be measured.", "That's a question for a textbook, not an experiment."]
      explain: "An investigable question names one thing you change (the thickness of the wrap) and one thing you measure (how fast the temperature falls)."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Which is the best hypothesis for that question?"
      options: ["If the wrap is thicker, the water will cool more slowly, because more trapped air slows conduction and blocks convection", "The wrap will make a difference", "Thicker wraps are better", "The water will cool down"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Too vague: what difference, and why?", "Better at what? A hypothesis names the relationship and gives a reason.", "That's true of every cup: it doesn't link the wrap to the cooling."]
      explain: "A good hypothesis states a relationship (thicker wrap, slower cooling), could be shown wrong by your data, and gives a reason from the model."
```

### The question

Scientists turn an idea from a model into something they can test. Here the idea is the trapped air from the last step: how would you test it with a cup of hot water, a thermometer and some wool?

## Evaluate: look back

```step
stage: info
check: { type: reflect, text: "I compared my prediction about the spoon with what the bar showed." }
```

Write one sentence: "At first I thought… Now I think… because…"

**Revision summary**

- **Conduction:** particles vibrate harder and pass energy to their neighbours by collisions. **The particles stay in place.** Mostly in solids; metals conduct well.
- **Convection:** heated fluid becomes less dense and rises, cooler fluid sinks: a **convection current**. **The particles move**, carrying the energy. Only in liquids and gases.
- **Insulators** (wood, plastic, trapped air) pass energy on poorly. Trapped air blocks convection too.
- It is the hot fluid that rises, not "heat".

```teacher
summary: Students explain conduction (energy passed by particle collisions,
  particles staying in place) and convection (the heated fluid itself moving,
  driven by density differences), and apply them to conductors and insulators
  (AC9S9U04, node 1).
time: 26
timing: Engage and Explore 8 min · Explain 11 min · Evaluate 3 min · Typical
  adds 3 min, Wider about 4 min
goals:
  - I can explain conduction as energy passed between particles by collisions.
  - I can explain convection as the movement of heated fluid, driven by density
    differences.
  - I can explain why a named material is a good conductor or a good insulator.
before: >
  A concept tutorial for introducing or revising the idea; it does not replace
  practical work. Set the width with `?width=minimum`, `typical` (default) or
  `wider`.


  The key contrast: in conduction, energy moves and particles don't; in
  convection, the particles carry the energy. Keep asking "what did one particle
  do?".


  Assumed: density from Year 7 (Properties: fewer particles in each cm³, less
  dense). The "Why it rises" question links it to convection and names the
  model's shortcut.


  Model note: in the simulation hot particles are pushed up directly; real hot
  fluid rises because its particles spread out (less dense). The wider step
  mentions possum-skin cloaks of south-eastern Australia; for richer context,
  use local resources and community guidance about First Nations clothing and
  bedding in your region.
running:
  - "Engage: ask who chose 'hot particles travel up the handle'. The bar answers
    it."
  - "Explore: on the bar, point to one particle for a few seconds. On the
    beaker, follow the ring the whole way round."
  - "Explain: the first two questions are the core; the sort applies them; 'why
    not in a solid' links back to Year 7 particle theory."
  - "In your own words: the comparison paragraph is the evidence for the node."
struggle: Seeing energy move while the particles stay put. When a student says
  particles travel along the bar, ask them to watch one particle in the middle
  for ten seconds.
stuck:
  - see: A student says heat rises.
    ask: On the board, what moved up?
    fix: Hot water, because it is less dense. Heat itself spreads in every direction
      (the bar conducted sideways).
  - see: A student says particles move along the bar.
    ask: Watch one particle in the middle for ten seconds. Where does it go?
    fix: "Nowhere: it vibrates in place. Only the energy travels."
  - see: A student says a metal bench is colder than a wooden one.
    ask: If both have been in the same room all day, what temperature are they?
    fix: The same. Metal feels colder because it conducts energy away from your hand
      faster.
stretch: Why is a heater usually placed low in a room and an air-conditioner high up?
support: "Give a two-column table (conduction, convection) with rows: what
  moves, which states, an example."
leads: >
  Next: the wave model of energy transfer: sound (node 2), then light and
  radiation (node 4).


  In class: wax-stuck pins along metal and wooden rods heated at one end; a
  convection tube or a beaker with potassium permanganate crystals heated at one
  side.
exit:
  q: Why can convection happen in water but not in a metal spoon?
  a: Convection needs the material to flow so heated parts can rise. Water's
    particles can move; a spoon's are held in place, so it can only conduct.
explain: >
  **Conduction:** particles vibrate harder and pass energy to their neighbours
  by collisions. The particles stay in place. Mostly in solids.


  **Convection:** heated fluid becomes less dense and rises; cooler fluid sinks.
  The particles carry the energy. Only in liquids and gases.
```
